messages.subject: How to export data as landmarks after estimate.missing function is used?
messages.subject_clean: How to export data as landmarks after estimate.missing function is used?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Colleagues,

I apologise if my question is too basic, but I have been stuck for a while now.

I am using estimate.missing() to estimate missing landmarks in a set of 160 individuals from an NTSYS file (I couldn't do the estimation using any other format), but I do not find the way of exporting the data or even read it further as landmark data in R.

So far, all works fine with the estimation. In the past, testing with few individuals I got good data back, but I exported using write.table(). This function was all I could find, but the array is not very "morphometrics-friendly" (each individual is represented by xyz columns as in morphologika, but the different individuals are next to each other). So I edited it by hand to a text or  morphologika file for further use. With 160 or more individuals, this option is not sensible.

Can you help me with this?

Thanks in advance,

Viviana

--

messages.body_plain:
Viviana,

the object resulting from applying estimate.missing includes the total dataset, with both previously full and newly estimated landmark positions, for all your specimens (see also the help file of the function). This object can be then used for analyses in R or be saved as a bin or as an Rdata file using save(). Alternatively, you can export it as a tps file using the function writland.tps(), or turn it into an nts-style 2D matrix using two.d.array and then save that as a table (using write.table).

Hope this helps
Antigoni

messages.subject: DA and asymetric components from bilat.symmetry
messages.subject_clean: DA and asymetric components from bilat.symmetry
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I used the bilat.symmetry function my dataset (53 landmarks, 688 individual) and got the DA component, but it has the dimensions (53,2,2). What does this represent? I would have thought it would give me some sort of output showing the average deviation of each point from it's paired point, and the average deviation of the unpaired points from the median line, but that wouldn't account for the 3rd dimension?

Also, what exactly is the asymmetric component of variation? I've read multiple sources but still don't understand - I get that the symmetric component is just a symmetrical version of the face, but what is the asymmetric component?

Cheers,

Richie

Please read the help file for the function a bit more carefully. Both of those are clearly described.

As to what the asymmetric component of shape variation represents, I suggest a read of the primary literature for that. It is explained in numerous publications on symmetry analysis of shape data.

I used the bilat.symmetry function my dataset (53 landmarks, 688 individual) and got the DA component, but it has the dimensions (53,2,2). What does this represent? I would have thought it would give me some sort of output showing the average deviation of each point from it's paired point, and the average deviation of the unpaired points from the median line, but that wouldn't account for the 3rd dimension?

Also, what exactly is the asymmetric component of variation? I've read multiple sources but still don't understand - I get that the symmetric component is just a symmetrical version of the face, but what is the asymmetric component?

Cheers,

Richie

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dean,

for DA component the help file reads "The directional asymmetry component, found as the mean shape for each side." I don't see how this corresponds to a 53 x 2 x 2 dataset. I get that the second and 3rd dimension are x,y and face side respectively, but each side of the face doesn't have 53 landmarks>?

Sorry, I I think I asked a different question to the one I wanted an answer for. The asymmetric component of variation is well described in the literature, but what isn't clear to me is how it relates to the output of the bilat.symmetry function. The symmetric component seems to be the aligned coordinates after the face has been made symmetrical, but I don't understand what the coordinates given by the asymmetric component represent?

Richie

messages.body_plain:
Ornella,

IN warpRefMesh, you must give it the name of the mesh Object. For your example that is

‘specimen1PLY’.  Instead you have given it the name of the PLY file “specimen1.ply”.  That is just a text file and is not in the proper format.

Instead try:

warpRefMesh“specimen1PLY, specimen1, average, color=NULL)

specimen1PLY <- read.ply("specimen1.ply", ShowSpecimen=TRUE) ### works

averagemesh <- warpRefMesh(“specimen1.ply”, specimen1, average, color=NULL) # this command does not work.

 I get the following message:

“Error in warpRefMesh("specimen1PLY.ply", specimen1,  :

  File is not a mesh3d object or xyz matrix”

For average, I followed the Geomorph guide and used the following:

average <-mshape(Y$coords) # ref

findMeanSpec(Y$coords)

I think that my “mesh.coord" and "ref” are x, y, z matrices but maybe they are not and I’m missing something. Originally my data is a morphologika file so I saved the specimen1 as a separate nts. file but maybe I didn’t formatted properly. Since it opens, I don’t understand where is the error.

Just to make sure for the “mesh.coord”, the data should be the raw data points for specimen1 but for the “ref”, they are the Procrustes coordinates for specimen1, is this correct?

Any ideas to resolve this issue? Sorry, I’m new to R so maybe I’m missing something fundamental.

Hello everyone,

I have a question about the wireframes in geomorph. I know it's possible to make your own wireframes in geomorph but I would like to import them instead.

  Coordinates must be a 3D array

I understand that my wireframes are not 3 dimensions but 2D. I went through the guide and I thought this was the way to have wireframes in your .txt file but maybe I am missing something (see attached the organization I followed in File1)

Does anyone know how to load wireframes? Should I make a different file?

Thanks in advance!

Ornella

messages.subject: How to perform a Procrustes ANOVA for specific groups?
messages.subject_clean: How to perform a Procrustes ANOVA for specific groups?
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I would like to perform a Procrustes Anova on my data. I managed to do it to a certain level but I get stuck. I looked through the guide and I could not find an answer but I'm probably missing something fundamental.

Here is my code:

gp <- as.factor(paste(classifier$Taxon))

gp2 <- as.factor(paste(classifier$Subfamily))

gp3 <- as.factor(paste(classifier$Family))

PCA <- plotTangentSpace(Y$coords, label=TRUE, verbose=TRUE, warpgrids = TRUE, groups=gp3)

gdf<-geomorph.data.frame(proc=Y$coords, CS=log(Y$Csize), subfamily = gp2, family = gp3, taxon = gp)

procD.lm(proc*CS ~ family, data=gdf,inter=10000)

My Procrustes ANOVA works for “family” but I would like to see it per individual families and not for “family” (i.e., family 1, family 2, family 3).

Something like this maybe? procD.lm(proc*CS ~ family1, data=gdf,inter=10000)

I understand that I’m missing a line of code to designate the names of the families that I would like to be analysed but I don’t know how to do it.

Maybe I should create something like that? “gp4 <- gp3 minus everything except family1” but I’m not sure how to do it.

Thanks in advance for your help!

Ornella

messages.body_plain:
Ornella,

If what you are asking is if the function can subset data for you, the answer is that it cannot.  You would have to subset your data first before running the analysis.  This is not a geomorph limitation - it would be true of almost any analytical function in R.  There would be no guide entry for this, I believe.  You might explore topics for subsetting data in R and once you figure that out, you would have to build separate geomorph data frames for your subsets.

Also, I’m not sure what the purpose is to assess a family effect with single families.  There is no variation to assess at that point.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.subject: Relationship with a continuing variable
messages.subject_clean: Relationship with a continuing variable
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

I am wondering how one would go about comparing morphological data with a continuing variable, other than size. Similar as can be done with tpsRegr. I have a number of populations of Arctic charr. I have compared their morphology using the ProcD.lm function. I have then further analysed the data using linear discriminant analysis. I am interested in creating deformation grids at the extreme of my discriminant axis's and add that to the plot. I can do this in tpsRegr, and add this using backwoods methods, e.g. in powerpoint. But I would be interested in doing this in R. Similarly one might be interested in other continuing variables to compare to shape, e.g. analyzing fork length, instead of centroid size, or environmental factors, e.g. temperature across populations etc.

I was wondering if the plotAllometry function could be used or if there are some other tricks to approach this.

Thank you in advance

Bjarni

messages.subject: Allometry and PCAs
messages.subject_clean: Allometry and PCAs
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm having some trouble in understanding the variation from my PCAs before and after the removal of allometry, which I'm hoping someone might be able to enlighten me where I am going wrong...

I have a single population with 89 offspring from 7 females, and I want to test whether offspring size (whole body) effects offspring head shape. I know individual size can often be used as an allometric measure, so I tested to see whether there was a correlation between Csize and offspring size, but there was not so will keep offspring size as one of my variables.

My PCA plot shows that PC1 explains 59% variation, and PC2 explains 14.5% of the variation. To check the loadings of each of my variables on each PC axis I ended up using linear models since I could not find this information in $rotation. Is there a better way than this? PC1 was significantly correlated with Csize (effect size of 3.673 sd) and PC2 was significantly correlated with size (effect size 5.103 sd).

Following this discussion closely (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/geomorph-r-package/1jXm_6dNE3A), my slopes were not biologically significant and I went ahead and obtained allometry-free shapes:

charrAllom <- procD.allometry(shape ~ Csize, ~ female, logsz = TRUE, data = gdf.symm, iter = 999)
charrAnova <- procD.lm(charrAllom$formula, data = charrAllom$data, iter = 999, RRPP = TRUE)
shape.resid <- arrayspecs(charrAnova$residuals, p = dim(gdf.symm$shape)[1], k = dim(gdf.symm$shape)[2]) # allometry adjusted residuals
# allometry free shapes
mean.shape <- mshape(gdf.symm$shape)
adj.shape <- shape.resid + array(mean.shape, dim(shape.resid))  # allometry-free shapes
PCA_noAllom <- plotTangentSpace(adj.shape, axis1 = 1, axis2 = 2, groups = gdf.symm$female)# PCA of allometry-free shape

The allometry-free PCA returned PC1 explaining 60.3% of the variation, and PC2 explaining 13.9% of the variation. None of which correlate with any of my variables. The shape change also changes little between my PCA with allometry, and PCA without allometry (see attached). If allometry was supposed to account for most of my variation in PC1, then I would expect a larger difference after the removal of allometry in my second PCA plot as well, which makes me think that the variation in PC1 was not due to allometry, or, I have made a mistake along the process.

Thanks in advance.

All the best,
Sam

Hi all,

So I am running into a similar issue with my 3D dataset. For some reason X coordinates are getting flipped and at the moment I can not identify the culprit. I've checked all the source files and their coordinates, I have also plotted each individual before GPA and all are aligned correctly. However, after GPA, several of my samples have their x-coordinate flipped (y and z seem to be okay). I'm worried that mean plots and the GPA composite of all samples may be influenced by these flipped coordinates. These coordinate flips create real problems when trying to compare deformation patterns resulting in useless data. Has anyone else run into this problem? Is there a solution? I would hate to have to force flip the coordinates of just flipped samples while others seem fine.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-GT01866GtC4/WqvcxwR1Q5I/AAAAAAAAUSQ/0Gng0YO8is8J_m1VZFlZr6ORq-UsPJrPQCLcBGAs/s1600/RawShape.png>

Fig1: 2D raw landmarks (z-axis removed) - red dot is the same LM tracked across all three figures.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-o85s8mPGLII/Wqvc3k1bTKI/AAAAAAAAUSU/oaAK6tKsQGcvLeaX-mkk-lsR8W0yl52xwCLcBGAs/s1600/GPAShape.png>

Fig 2: 2D coordinates after GPA for the same individual in Fig 1.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-WMWHYzcsbEs/Wqvc6loaS6I/AAAAAAAAUSY/EVTnETI7RgMUwx6IdFayhCNvNQCUTAUdgCLcBGAs/s1600/MeanShape.png>

Fig 3: 2D mean shape for the group that individual 6 belongs. Notice the mean shape is flipped (position of the red dot) in relation to Fig 2. All GPA 2D coordinates from all individuals from this group are oriented as in Fig 2, so why is the mean shape flipped?

Cheers,
Jeremy

messages.body_plain:
Jeremy,

The GPA function in geomorph will not automatically reflect specimens during the analysis (one form of flipping). What I meant in my earlier post was that some of the specimens may be digitized as R or L.  Combining them makes little sense in their original; one must reflect them prior to GPA.

Note that your 2D view of these by simply excising the Z coordinate is not a perfect way to see any issues, because GPA will rotate in all 3 dimensions. Thus the X,Y,Z axes are not the same before and after GPA.

I suggest you examine closely your original specimens to ensure that they are not ‘righties’ and ‘lefties’ before combining them and submitting them to a GPA.

Dean

I've checked all the source files and their coordinates, I have also plotted each individual before GPA and all are aligned correctly. However, after GPA, several of my samples have their x-coordinate flipped (y and z seem to be okay). I'm worried that mean plots and the GPA composite of all samples may be influenced by these flipped coordinates. I would hate to have to force flip the coordinates of just flipped samples while others seem fine.

messages.body_plain:
Sam,

“The allometry-free PCA returned PC1 explaining 60.3% of the variation, and PC2 explaining 13.9% of the variation. None of which correlate with any of my variables. The shape change also changes little between my PCA with allometry, and PCA without allometry (see attached). If allometry was supposed to account for most of my variation in PC1, then I would expect a larger difference after the removal of allometry in my second PCA plot as well, which makes me think that the variation in PC1 was not due to allometry, or, I have made a mistake along the process. “

The a priori intuition in your statement above is misguided. There is no reason that allometry must account for most variation in any dataset, nor that it align perfectly with PC1.  PCA does not ‘find’ a particular biological factor; it merely rotates data to the direction of maximal variation. That direction could associate with allometry, group differences, elevation, or NOTHING. Thus any expectation that PC1 ‘shows’ some biological factor should be avoided. It is a rotation-based visualization tool, not factor exploration (for the latter try factor analysis).

Second, while it is unclear what you mean by ‘expect a larger difference after the removal of allometry’, remember that the 2 PCAs are performed on different datasets (original and size-residuals). Your question implies that comparing the percentage of variation across axes across analyses is useful and meaningful. It is not, because these are based on datasets containing differing totals of variation (by definition the size-residuals have less variation than the original data). There is simply no way of knowing what percentage of variation will be on PC1, PC2 or any axis when comparing them. I know of no statistical theory that would generate any expectation in this regard, as the pattern of variation and covariation in the second dataset is conditioned on size while the former is not.

The PCA analyses know nothing about other sources of variation, so it is unclear how one could derive an expectation of % variation across PC axes without the biologist having that knowledge to establish it.

Dean

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Director of Graduate Education, EEB Program

Professor

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

       Department of Statistics

Iowa State University

Subject: [geomorph-r-package] Allometry and PCAs

Hi everyone,

I'm having some trouble in understanding the variation from my PCAs before and after the removal of allometry, which I'm hoping someone might be able to enlighten me where I am going wrong...

I have a single population with 89 offspring from 7 females, and I want to test whether offspring size (whole body) effects offspring head shape. I know individual size can often be used as an allometric measure, so I tested to see whether there was a correlation between Csize and offspring size, but there was not so will keep offspring size as one of my variables.

My PCA plot shows that PC1 explains 59% variation, and PC2 explains 14.5% of the variation. To check the loadings of each of my variables on each PC axis I ended up using linear models since I could not find this information in $rotation. Is there a better way than this? PC1 was significantly correlated with Csize (effect size of 3.673 sd) and PC2 was significantly correlated with size (effect size 5.103 sd).

Following this discussion closely (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/geomorph-r-package/1jXm_6dNE3A), my slopes were not biologically significant and I went ahead and obtained allometry-free shapes:

charrAllom <- procD.allometry(shape ~ Csize, ~ female, logsz = TRUE, data = gdf.symm, iter = 999)

charrAnova <- procD.lm(charrAllom$formula, data = charrAllom$data, iter = 999, RRPP = TRUE)

shape.resid <- arrayspecs(charrAnova$residuals, p = dim(gdf.symm$shape)[1], k = dim(gdf.symm$shape)[2]) # allometry adjusted residuals

# allometry free shapes

mean.shape <- mshape(gdf.symm$shape)

adj.shape <- shape.resid + array(mean.shape, dim(shape.resid))  # allometry-free shapes

PCA_noAllom <- plotTangentSpace(adj.shape, axis1 = 1, axis2 = 2, groups = gdf.symm$female)# PCA of allometry-free shape

The allometry-free PCA returned PC1 explaining 60.3% of the variation, and PC2 explaining 13.9% of the variation. None of which correlate with any of my variables. The shape change also changes little between my PCA with allometry, and PCA without allometry (see attached). If allometry was supposed to account for most of my variation in PC1, then I would expect a larger difference after the removal of allometry in my second PCA plot as well, which makes me think that the variation in PC1 was not due to allometry, or, I have made a mistake along the process.

Thanks in advance.

All the best,

Sam

messages.body_plain:
Jeremy,

You might consider not aligning your specimens to their principal components or just recognize that if you do these analyses separately for each population, an arbitrary outcome might make the alignment of one group turned 180 degrees compared to another.  This is a common outcome with PCA.  The principal components can be turned 180 degrees and the result is no different (you just change the way you look at it).  It just looks different because it is happening arbitrarily by group.

Why you are running GPA separately on groups and attempting to compare populations is a whole other problem that you should reconsider.  I’m not sure I understand the logic in that.

Cheers!
Mike

My data is split up into several different populations but when I do a GPA across all specimen, they seem to all be in the same orientation; however, if separated into their populations, after GPA the realignment is very apparent (x-coordinates flipped for some individuals resulting in population means to be flipped). messages.body_plain:
Mike,

Thank you for the quick reply. In my overall analysis, I'm using the superimposition from GPA to investigate the effects of population and other covariates on shape with ProcD.lm. However, in order to understand how each population differs from each other I generate mean shapes for each population to compare using plotRefToTarget. Perhaps this has been the problem. I suppose that instead of regenerating the superimposition or using mshape by each population, I could pull out, from the original overall GPA, the aligned coordinates for individuals and separate them by population and generate a mean this way. This could work, as in the larger GPA, the point cloud doesn't seem to show signs of specimen flipping. I never thought about doing it this way because I thought it would be better to generate mean shapes from each population separately. Does this approach sound reasonable?

Cheers,
Jeremy

messages.body_plain:
Jeremy,

The function, coords.subset, has an example on the help page to do exactly what you wish to do. There is no reason to secondarily run GPA on your separate populations. In fact, there are several arguments for why not to do this, one of which you have already discovered.

Good luck!
Mike

Sent from my iPhone

On Mar 19, 2018, at 8:16 AM, Jeremy Gibson <jeremy....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Mike,
>
> Thank you for the quick reply. In my overall analysis, I'm using the superimposition from GPA to investigate the effects of population and other covariates on shape with ProcD.lm. However, in order to understand how each population differs from each other I generate mean shapes for each population to compare using plotRefToTarget. Perhaps this has been the problem. I suppose that instead of regenerating the superimposition or using mshape by each population, I could pull out, from the original overall GPA, the aligned coordinates for individuals and separate them by population and generate a mean this way. This could work, as in the larger GPA, the point cloud doesn't seem to show signs of specimen flipping. I never thought about doing it this way because I thought it would be better to generate mean shapes from each population separately. Does this approach sound reasonable?
>
> Cheers,
> Jeremy
>
> On Monday, March 19, 2018 at 11:42:26 AM UTC, Michael Collyer wrote:
> > Jeremy,
> >
> > You might consider not aligning your specimens to their principal components or just recognize that if you do these analyses separately for each population, an arbitrary outcome might make the alignment of one group turned 180 degrees compared to another.  This is a common outcome with PCA.  The principal components can be turned 180 degrees and the result is no different (you just change the way you look at it).  It just looks different because it is happening arbitrarily by group.

> > Why you are running GPA separately on groups and attempting to compare populations is a whole other problem that you should reconsider.  I’m not sure I understand the logic in that.

messages.body_plain:
Jeremy,

Mike caught an important component that I missed in your posts: the separate GPA. Definitely do not do this. Instead, a single GPA of all specimens followed by subsetting as Mike suggested is what is appropriate.

Note also that one can obtain the group means from an anova model using advanced.procD.lm. That is yet another approach to getting where you wish to be.

Good luck,

Dean

Director of Graduate Education, EEB Program

Professor

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Jeremy,

The function, coords.subset, has an example on the help page to do exactly what you wish to do. There is no reason to secondarily run GPA on your separate populations. In fact, there are several arguments for why not to do this, one of which you have already discovered.

Good luck!

Mike

Sent from my iPhone

However, in order to understand how each population differs from each other I generate mean shapes for each population to compare using plotRefToTarget. Perhaps this has been the problem. I suppose that instead of regenerating the superimposition or using mshape by each population, I could pull out, from the original overall GPA, the aligned coordinates for individuals and separate them by population and generate a mean this way. This could work, as in the larger GPA, the point cloud doesn't seem to show signs of specimen flipping. I never thought about doing it this way because I thought it would be better to generate mean shapes from each population separately. Does this approach sound reasonable?

> >

> >
> > You might consider not aligning your specimens to their principal components or just recognize that if you do these analyses separately for each population, an arbitrary outcome might make the alignment of one group turned 180 degrees compared to another.  This is a common outcome with PCA.  The principal components can be turned 180 degrees and the result is no different (you just change the way you look at it). messages.body_plain:
Mike and Dean,

Thanks so much for the comments - Yep, the population based PGA was definitely the problem. Now with individuals separated out by population from the overall GPA, all samples and mean shapes are oriented in the same direction - yeah! Now looking back at my code - it is a very good lesson to pass things by others - I got into a coding zone and just applied GPA analysis to each population and didn't think anything more about - that is until I wanted to start comparing mean shapes. Fortunately, I was not using those results in my overall statistical models. Thanks so much for the quick feedback - very much appreciated!

Cheers,
Jeremy

messages.body_plain:
Sérgio,

At present, there is no correct way of doing non-BM ancestral state estimation for multivariate data.

For multivariate data, all presently proposed methods for evaluating non-Brownian motion evolutionary models (e.g., OU, EB, etc.) display very high rates of misspecification (type I error). That is, they find strong support for more complex models than were used to generate the data (e.g., generate multivariate data under BM, and the methods find strong support for OU). This is undesirable to say the least, and some methods are even worse than this!  A recent review of the problems is found in Adams and Collyer, 2018: Systematic Biology.

By extension of these results, working ‘backwards’ to estimate ancestral states using anything except BM will not work as intended.

At the present time, if one wishes to make correct inferences with multivariate data, one is restricted to Brownian motion.

Dean

messages.subject: Removing the effects of size
messages.subject_clean: Removing the effects of size
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

There is one thing I´m wondering about, and perhaps you could come up with some ideas regarding this.  I  am studying morphological variation among different populations of small benthic charr in Iceland.  I have run a morphometric analysis and found out that size is a significant factor in explaining the morphology of these fish.

Datafr.gdf<-geomorph.data.frame(cave.gpa, caves=caves)
procD.lm(coords~log(Csize),iter=999, data=Datafr.gdf)

I tested if the slopes were homogneous, They were not, but there was no systematic variation when comparing across populations.

Morph.disgroups<-morphol.disparity(coords~log(Csize)*caves, groups=~caves, data=Datafr.gdf, iter=999)

I took size in to account when comparing morphology of these fish.

procD.lm(coords~log(Csize)+caves,iter=999, data=Datafr.gdf)

I think all of this is correct way of doing things.   Now I am interested in two things one to describe the differences among the caves using discriminant function analysis's. There I am mostly interested in how well fish can be classified to their own population, and where the mis-classified fish end up. Second I´m interested in the morphological variation among the caves using PCA -

PCA<-plotTangentSpace(cave.gpa$coords, verbose =T).

In both cases I can visualize morphology at the extreem of either PCA or DFA axises, using.
e.g.

DF1pred<-shape.predictor(cave.gpa$coords,Pred.Discr$x[,1], Intercept=FALSE, pred1=-3, pred2=3 )
Mean_morph<-mshape(cave.gpa$coords)
plotRefToTarget(Mean_morph, DF1pred$pred1) #min
plotRefToTarget(Mean_morph, DF1pred$pred2) #max

But how do I remove the effect of size from these visualization?  Can I calculate the residuals of each landmark from a regression of landmark scores and log Centroid size and then use those for such visualization? Similarily, can I use such residual landmarks for the DFA analysis and the PCA calculations?  I´m not planing to do any statistical analysis with the PCA scores, only for visualization of  how mean scores of populations are distributed, and how that is related to morphology.

Thanks in advance

Bjarni

messages.body_plain:
Dear Bjarni,

yes, one could take the residuals of a linear model for further analyses, and those residuals would be "corrected" for the terms included in the model. You would just need to add back the consensus for visualization, because the residuals are from a model that includes an intercept and will not resemble the structure you are studying unless you do that.

Of course, some thinking is required to decide which is the model you want to use, especially if you have different slopes for your groups. BTW, morphol.disparity does not test for homogeneity of slopes, please consult the help file of that function carefully. Also notice that the statistics of a discriminant analysis are MANOVA statistics, and will thus give you the same answer as a linear model (although I would argue that using procD.lm for that also gives you the advantage of hypothesis testing based on permutation of residuals).

Hope this helps
Antigoni

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Removing the effects of size
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Removing the effects of size
messages.body_plain:
Bjarni,

As Antigoni mentioned, one can use residuals (plus average shape) as allometry-corrected shapes, but this should only true if one establishes that a common-allometry model is appropriate; i.e., shape ~ size + group.  If you find you have heterogenous allometries ( shape ~ size + group + size x group is a better model), then you cannot correct for allometry.

It seems you desire to perform DFA is for classification of individuals to groups?  If you have heterogenous allometries, you must realize that it is insufficient to ask, “To which group should this individual be classified based on its shape?”  Rather, you must then ask, “To which group should this individual be classified based on its shape, given its size?”  The latter recognizes that the classification posterior probabilities are much more complex, as prior probabilities are based on group shape distinction as it varies with size.  For example, maybe at small sizes, one cannot predict group but at larger sizes it becomes easier.

If you have heterogenous allometries, please try to abandon a lumping or splitting focus and focus more so on whether groups converge in shape or diverge in shape as they grow larger.  This is what a model with significant variation in allometries among groups would encourage you to do.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Sergio,

>
>
> For instance, with my data they retreave different results. I don't completely understand what is the difference between f1=shape ~ log(cs)+gp, f2=~log(cs)*gp and f1=shape ~ log(cs), f2=~log(cs)*gp.

The former has a null model with different intercepts for groups and tests only the interaction, which is homogeneity of slopes test.  The latter forces all groups to have the same intercept in the null model (no groups at all) and tests the variation associated with different group slopes AND intercepts.  This is not a homogeneity of slopes test.  It is a test to compare a global allometry to individual group allometries.  A homogeneity of slopes test normally allows for different intercepts.  A subtle but distinctly different set of tests.

Arguments could be made for doing either, but the point is that if the variation is significant, one should not look for ways to remove allometric variation but instead focus on WHY the variation is significant, which you did with your pairwise arguments (groups and slope).

Cheers!
Mike

messages.subject_clean: Multivariate regression of non-coordinate data using procD.lm
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm trying to perform an allometric space analysis (PCA) based on the coefficients of a multivariate regression of my raw data (i.e. linear measurements). I have 24 shape variables and 1 size variable, and roughly 60 specimens from 9 species. Since I need the coefficients of my shape variables I ran the regression as size~shape, instead of shape~size (which is the basic structure recommended for procD.lm).

Now, when I try to do this for a specific species (n=14) I try the following:
(lm<-procD.lm(size~shape1+shape2+shape3...shape24,data = data[[1]]$`speciesname`,effect.type=c("F"),RRPP = TRUE,iter = 9999)

And I get the following error:

Error in array(x, c(length(x), 1L), if (!is.null(names(x))) list(names(x),  :
  'data' must be of a vector type, was 'NULL'

I'm guessing that it's because I have more shape variables than samples, so I tried running the same including fewer variables, and it works until I include n-1 shape variables.
I know of previous works that have used the same method and they were able to use this function to run a multivariate regression in this same scenario (i.e. fewer samples than shape variables). Can anyone point out my rookie mistake that I seem to miss?

Thanks in advanced!
Camilo

messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Multivariate regression of non-coordinate data using procD.lm
messages.body_plain:
Camillo,

The problem is likely caused by the fact that you have more shape variables than the rank of a matrix of shape variables.  If n = 14, then the maximum rank of a matrix of variables for describing the data of the 14 specimens is 13.  For example, if you were to do a PCA on what you are calling the shape variables, only 13 eigenvalues would be positive, meaning you only need 13 principal components to fully capture all the variation in your data.

The error happens because you started adding null dimensions to your linear model design matrix. Behind the scenes, procD.lm uses QR decomposition on design matrices to get the model rank (degrees of freedom).  After you added 13 variables, adding additional variables did not change the rank of the QR decomposition (0 degrees fo freedom added), so an error occurred when R tried to make a vector of nothing.

Another way to do this that might not spring an error is

fit <- procD.lm(size ~ shape, …)
fit$coefficients

where shape is the full matrix of 24 “shape” variables.  This might not cause an error, but you will only have 13 rows in your matrix of coefficients (not counting the intercept).

I do not fully understand the purpose of your analysis and I am not sure how you derived your size variable.  So a better question might be, “Why are you trying to predict size from shape?”  If this is an appropriate thing to do, you just have to realize that the shape variables are not independent of each other and should be limited in number to n - 1; i.e., the dimensions of your data space.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Ornella,

You are correct that the rotation differs slightly at present. The reason is that the PCA for phylomorphospace is currently obtained for both the extant and estimated ancestors. This is fine, as it is just a small rotational difference from the PCA of extant taxa only. It also does not alter the relationships among taxa, as the distances in either fully rotated space are identical.  However, I admit that this is a bit inelegant.

Currently, we are working on an alternative approach and a new function where the PCA is performed on the extant taxa only, and the ancestral estimates projected into the space. This way, the PCA and phylomorphospace PCA will show the same exact plot with or without the ancestors. We do not yet have this function ready at this time, but hope to roll it out sometime soon.

Best,

Dean

Hello everyone,

I have a question related to the physignal function. I want to make sure that I'm doing it properly.

I have used the following command for my entire tree:

physignal(Y$coords,mytree,iter = 9999)

Now I would like to check the phylogenetic signal for specific clades, I have made a subset tree and and subset of my procrustes coordinates for a specific group:

YcoordSb<- Y$coords[,,1:22]

mytreeSb<-read.tree(file ="mytree2.tre")

physignal(YcoordSb,mytreeSb,iter = 9999)

However, I would like to know if there is a way to select a particular clade instead of creating a separate tree file. So I have created a variable that only include a specific clade using my original tree:

Clade1<-tips(mytree, mrca(mytree)["taxonA","taxonB"])

This returns all the taxa belonging to Clade 1; however I'm having a hard time integrating it into the phylosignal function, I tried something like that but it does not work:

physignal(YcoordSb,mytree$Clade1,iter = 9999)

Thank you so much for all the help you are providing to people like me! Thank you for taking the time to answer all our questions.

Ornella

messages.body_plain:
Ornella,

You need to match up the subset of species in the data with a pruned phylogeny. The following procedure is one way:

1: create reduced dataset: example: mydat.small<-mydata[,,1:22]

2: use the ‘treedata’ function In geiger to match reduced data  to tree:

  Matchdata<-treedata(phy = origphylogeny, data = mydat.small)

plot(Matchdata$phy)  #check to see that the pruned tree is what you want

3: physignal(mydat.small, Matchdata$phy)

messages.subject: Need help with an error in two.b.pls.
messages.subject_clean: Need help with an error in two.b.pls.
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

My name is Eddie Gadee, I attended the PR Statistics Geomorph workshop in Wales this past month, and I was wondering if I can get some help or clarification on a small error I am receiving in a Geomorph command. I'm currently trying to conduct a two.b.pls command on some GPA-aligned arrays.

My work, in detail, is as follows: I have 6 specimens/.ply files of a certain bone found in a bird species I am investigating. For each specimen, I am digitizing 3 sets of landmarks. One set is the superior region of the bone (abbreviated as cg), one set is the midsection (bh), and the third set is the inferior portion of the bone (pc). I've digitized 6 landmarks for each specimen's cg part, 12 for each specimen's bh, and 10 for each pc. Now that I have .nts files for all of the landmarks I placed, I sorted them into 3 folders respectively (cg, bh, pc) and each folder contains a uniform 6 files/specimens.

I then created respective filelists for the files in each of the folders (cg.data, bh.data, pc.data), read them into R, and successfully performed gpagen on all 3 of the filelists. Now I want to perform a two.b.pls on all 3 arrays (which I am aware is possible and calls for other functions to be performed later on that I can do). Doing this for 3 arrays warrants this command being done between all 3 arrays anyway (cg,bh; cg,pc; bh,pc). The only problem is, when I enter my code as follows, I get this error:

> two.b.pls(cg.data[,,1], pc.data[,,1], iter=999)
Error in two.b.pls(cg.data[, , 1], pc.data[, , 1], iter = 999) :
  Data matrices have different numbers of specimens.

While the error message sounds pretty straightforward, I am nonetheless confused because each one of my arrays do indeed contain a uniform amount of 6 specimens, and I don't understand what I am supposed to diagnose here. I verified that the amount of specimens are the same. The only thing I can guess is that by specimens, R is referring to landmarks? Could it be that R is telling me that each of my arrays need to have specimens that have the same number of landmarks, and not have one array of 6-landmarked specimens, one array of 12-landmarked specimens, and one of 10-landmarked specimens? This would mean I have to redigitize, which is time-consuming but okay, but I just want to confirm if my hunch is on the right track or if this is an error that I am not really understanding entirely. Any solution to being able to resolve this error and perform this command would be really helpful.

Thank you very much!

- Eddie

messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Need help with an error in two.b.pls.
messages.body_plain:
Hi Eddie,

the error message is meant to transmit exactly what you are interpreting, a different number of specimens. If dim(cg.data) and dim(pc.data) give you the same third element (i.e. the number of specimens) you should be OK.

Note however, that in your code you are passing to the function an index of the first specimen of each dataset (through [,,1]) which means that you are trying to run a pls with only one specimen. This is not possible, and it might be triggering the error you are seeing. Try to remove that and see if the function now works.

Hope this helps

Antigoni

messages.body_plain:
Ornella,

If you have names for each object, these are found in the ‘third’ dimension of ‘dimnames’.  For instance, try:

library(geomorph)

data(plethspecies)

plethspecies$land

dimnames(plethspecies$land)  #shown another way.

If you then reduce part of the data, the names will come along with it, for instance:

plethspecies$land[,,1:3]

Check to see if your original data contained these names; that may be the problem.

Dean

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I'm running into a problem that might actually be easy to fix but as a new R user, I'm having a hard time finding what I should do. I know it's possible to select a certain number of your Procrustes coordinates with Y$coords[,,1:10] but what I would like to do is to select [,,1:4] and [,,17:20] at once without creating two separate variables, in the same way as in GroupA<-gp[c(1:4,17:20)]

I have been trying several ways such as:
> YcoordA<- Y$coords[,,1:4],[,,17:20]
Error: unexpected ',' in "YcoordA<- Y$coords[,,1:4],"

The reason, I'm trying to do that is because I would like to compare two groups using the ProcD function and if I try something else such as creating two different groups A(1:4) and B(17:20), I get the following error:

> Group<-gp[c(1:4,17:20)]

> YcoordA<- Y$coords[,,1:4]

> YcoordB<-Y$coords[,,17:20]

> YCsize<- Y$Csize[c(1:4,17:20)]

> gdf<-geomorph.data.frame(proc= YcoordA, YcoordB, CS=log(YCsizeA), gp1=Group)

Error in geomorph.data.frame(proc = YcoordA, YcoordB, CS = log(YCsize),  :

  Inputs have different numbers of observations

It might not be possible or there is a crucial step that I'm missing.

Thanks in advance for your help!

Ornella

Hi Antigoni,

Thanks for reaching out. When I remove the [,,1] from the code, this is the error I get:

> two.b.pls(cg.data, pc.data, iter=999)
Error in y[rownames(x), ] : subscript out of bounds

This is actually the code I tried initially, and I only added the [,,1] on my own after seeing this error and wondering if this would fix the error. The reason I tried this is because the first two dimensions of my data appeared as "null" when I entered dimnames, but even so, the third dimension of both sets have the same number of specimens:

> dimnames(cg.data)
[[1]]
NULL

[[2]]
NULL

[[3]]
[1] "CHLOROSTEJ162Landcg" "HEMPARV162Landcg"    "hemVir179413Landcg"
[4] "LCAER148Landcg"      "palmDolLandcg"       "VESTCOC146Landcg"

> dimnames(pc.data)
[[1]]
NULL

[[2]]
NULL

[[3]]
[1] "CHLOROSTEJ162Landpc" "HEMPARV162Landpc"    "hemVir179413Landpc"
[4] "LCAER148Landpc"      "palmDolLandpc"       "VESTCOC146Landpc"

Hopefully this information is useful.

-Eddie

On Friday, March 30, 2018 at 4:05:00 AM UTC-4, Antigoni Kaliontzopoulou wrote:

> Hi Eddie,
>
> the error message is meant to transmit exactly what you are interpreting, a different number of specimens. If dim(cg.data) and dim(pc.data) give you the same third element (i.e. the number of specimens) you should be OK.
>
> Note however, that in your code you are passing to the function an index of the first specimen of each dataset (through [,,1]) which means that you are trying to run a pls with only one specimen. This is not possible, and it might be triggering the error you are seeing. Try to remove that and see if the function now works.
>
> Hope this helps
>
> Antigoni
>
> On 30/03/2018 05:54, lostle...@gmail.com wrote:

> > Hi everyone,
> >
> >
> > My name is Eddie Gadee, I attended the PR Statistics Geomorph workshop in Wales this past month, and I was wondering if I can get some help or clarification on a small error I am receiving in a Geomorph command. I'm currently trying to conduct a two.b.pls command on some GPA-aligned arrays.
> >
> >
> >
> > My work, in detail, is as follows: I have 6 specimens/.ply files of a certain bone found in a bird species I am investigating. For each specimen, I am digitizing 3 sets of landmarks. One set is the superior region of the bone (abbreviated as cg), one set is the midsection (bh), and the third set is the inferior portion of the bone (pc). I've digitized 6 landmarks for each specimen's cg part, 12 for each specimen's bh, and 10 for each pc. Now that I have .nts files for all of the landmarks I placed, I sorted them into 3 folders respectively (cg, bh, pc) and each folder contains a uniform 6 files/specimens.
> >
> >
> >
> > I then created respective filelists for the files in each of the folders (cg.data, bh.data, pc.data), read them into R, and successfully performed gpagen on all 3 of the filelists. Now I want to perform a two.b.pls on all 3 arrays (which I am aware is possible and calls for other functions to be performed later on that I can do). Doing this for 3 arrays warrants this command being done between all 3 arrays anyway (cg,bh; cg,pc; bh,pc). The only problem is, when I enter my code as follows, I get this error:
> >
> >
> > > two.b.pls(cg.data[,,1], pc.data[,,1], iter=999)
> > Error in two.b.pls(cg.data[, , 1], pc.data[, , 1], iter = 999) :
> >   Data matrices have different numbers of specimens.
> >
> > While the error message sounds pretty straightforward, I am nonetheless confused because each one of my arrays do indeed contain a uniform amount of 6 specimens, and I don't understand what I am supposed to diagnose here. I verified that the amount of specimens are the same. The only thing I can guess is that by specimens, R is referring to landmarks? Could it be that R is telling me that each of my arrays need to have specimens that have the same number of landmarks, and not have one array of 6-landmarked specimens, one array of 12-landmarked specimens, and one of 10-landmarked specimens? This would mean I have to redigitize, which is time-consuming but okay, but I just want to confirm if my hunch is on the right track or if this is an error that I am not really understanding entirely. Any solution to being able to resolve this error and perform this command would be really helpful.
> >
> >
> >
> > Thank you very much!
> >
> >
> >
> > - Eddie

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I'm running into a problem with my morphologika file. I have two files, which are exactly the same except that one has the wireframe at the end.

When I run the one with the wireframe (dataset A), dim is NULL:
> dim(mydata)
NULL
> str(mydata)
List of 2
 $ coords   : num [1:30, 1:3, 1:32] 19.2 15.3 20.1 20.2 17.8 ...
  ..- attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 3
  .. ..$ : NULL
  .. ..$ : NULL
  .. ..$ : chr [1:32] "Species_1" "Species_2" "Species_3" "Species_4" ...
 $ wireframe: num [1:36, 1:2] 1 1 1 2 3 3 3 4 6 6 ...
> Y <- gpagen(mydata$coords, Proj = TRUE, PrinAxes = TRUE)
  |
  |                                                                                      |   0%
  |
  |=================                                                                     |  20%
  |
  |==================================                                                    |  40%
  |
  |====================================================                                  |  60%
  |
  |======================================================================================| 100%

The gpagen works fine and I can run all my subsequent anaylses with the Y$coords.

Dataset B without wireframes, dim is not NULL but cannot run gpagen:
> dim(mydata2)
[1] 30  3 32
> str(mydata2)
 num [1:30, 1:3, 1:32] 19.2 15.3 20.1 20.2 17.8 ...
 - attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 3
  ..$ : NULL
  ..$ : NULL
  ..$ : chr [1:32] "Species_1" "Species_2" "Species_3" "Species_4" ...
> Y <- gpagen(mydata2$coords, Proj = TRUE, PrinAxes = TRUE)
Error in mydata2$coords : $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors

I'm really confused why one is working and the other is not. Two other colleagues in my lab, have ran into the exact same problem with different datasets. I have been using the dataset A (with wireframes), which has been good but now I want to use a function that needs the "dimnames" and since they are NULL, it does not work. I have attached a template of how my dataset is organized.

If anyone has an idea of why this is happening and how to fix it, I would be really grateful because I ran out of ideas myself being quite a novice in R.

Thank you in advance for your help!

Ornella
